questions.title: Why does the token‑level importance ratio in GRPO lead to high‑variance gradients?
questions.question_body: In GRPO the importance ratio is defined as $w_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\theta(y_{i,t}\big|x,y_{i,<t})}{\theta_{\text{old}}(y_{i,t}\big|x,y_{i,<t})}$. The paper claims that this is a misuse of importance sampling because it applies a single‑sample weight to each token. Can someone explain, with a small example, how this single‑token weighting breaks the expectation‑correctness of importance sampling and why that causes the gradient variance to blow up as the output length increases?

questions.title: How exactly does length‑normalisation in $s_i(\theta)$ reduce variance?
questions.question_body: GSPO defines the sequence‑level importance ratio as $s_{i}(\theta)=\big(\frac{\theta(y_i|x)}{\theta_{\text{old}}(y_i|x)}\big)^{1/|y_i|}$. The authors say this normalises by the sequence length to keep $s_i(\theta)$ in a unified range. Could someone derive the variance of $s_i(\theta)$ with and without this exponent for a toy distribution? Why does this particular form avoid the extreme fluctuations that would otherwise happen when a few token log‑probabilities differ?

questions.title: What is the relationship between GRPO's clipping range and GSPO's clipping range?
questions.question_body: GRPO uses $\text{clip}(w_{i,t},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$ with $\text{min}(w_{i,t}\tilde A_{i,t},\text{clip}(...))$, and GSPO uses $\text{clip}(s_i,1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$. The paper notes that the magnitude of these ratios, and hence the appropriate $\text{min/clip}$, differ by orders of magnitude. How can we formally relate the two sets of importance ratios and understand why a tiny GSPO clipping interval (e.g. $3\times10^{-4}$) is appropriate while a GRPO interval of $0.2$ is not?

questions.title: Why does GSPO avoid the need for a value model?
questions.question_body: PPO typically requires a value model to estimate the advantage $\tilde A_t$. GSPO replaces this with a group‑based advantage that uses the standardised reward over a batch of responses. In what scenarios does GRPO fail without a value model, and how does the group standardisation in GSPO effectively replace the value estimate? Does GSPO suffer from any bias because it only uses relative rewards within a group?

questions.title: What exactly is the ‘expert‑activation volatility’ problem in MoE models that GRPO encounters?
questions.question_body: The paper explains that after a gradient update, about 10% of the experts activated on a given token change between $\theta$ and $\theta_{\text{old}}$. Why does this volatility make token‑level importance ratios unreliable? Can we derive an expression showing how a change in expert selection amplifies the variance of $w_{i,t}(\theta)$? Also, how does GSPO’s reliance on sequence‑likelihood make it immune to this issue?

questions.title: Why are the advantages $A_{i,t}$ in GSPO‑token identical to the sequence‑level advantage $A_i$?
questions.question_body: Equation (9) in the paper shows that GSPO‑token and GSPO are numerically identical when $\tilde A_{i,t}=\tilde A_{i}$ for all tokens. Could someone walk through the algebra that shows $s_{i,t}(\theta)$ reduces to $s_i(\theta)$ using the `sg` operation, and explain why this makes the two objectives the same? What practical difference does this have if we actually set $\tilde A_{i,t}$ to different values per token?

questions.title: Is the gradient of GSPO equivalent to that of a simple likelihood ratio policy gradient?
questions.question_body:
Equation (8) gives the GSPO gradient as $
abla_\theta J_{\text{GSPO}} = \frac{1}{G}\big(\frac{\theta(y_i|x)}{\theta_{\text{old}}(y_i|x)}\big)^{1/|y_i|}\tilde A_i \frac{1}{|y_i|}
abla_\theta\big(\frac{1}{|y_i|}\big)\frac{\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}{\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}$. Ignoring clipping, how does this compare to the classic REINFORCE update $
abla_\theta J = \frac{\theta(y_i|x)}{\theta_{\text{old}}(y_i|x)}\tilde A_i 
abla_\theta\theta(y_i|x)$? What role does the $1/|y_i|$ factor play?

questions.title: How does GSPO handle very long generation lengths without exploding variance?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that GSPO remains stable even when the expected response length increases, whereas GRPO collapses. Can someone provide a theoretical explanation (or a simulation sketch) showing how the variance of the sequence‑level importance ratio scales with $|y_i|$ compared to the token‑level ratio? Does normalising by $|y_i|$ fully eliminate the length‑dependent variance?

questions.title: Can GSPO be trivially extended to multi‑turn dialogue with token‑level objectives?
questions.question_body: GSPO-token offers a token‑level objective for multi‑turn RL. How would one set up the group‑based advantage for a dialogue consisting of multiple turns? Is there a risk that the per‑turn standardisation reduces the signal at earlier turns? What practical tricks might mitigate this?

questions.title: What is the impact of using inference‑engine likelihoods for GSPO optimization?
questions.question_body: Section 4.4 mentions that GSPO is tolerant to precision discrepancies between training and inference engines, allowing the reuse of likelihoods from the inference engine. In practice, how significant can rounding or quantisation differences be, and how does GSPO’s sequence‑level ratio mitigate the resulting bias? Would you recommend any specific precision settings or post‑processing steps?

questions.title: Is GSPO theoretically guaranteed to converge under the same assumptions as PPO?
questions.question_body: PPO’s convergence analysis relies on certain assumptions about the clipping region and the boundedness of advantage estimates. Does GSPO share these assumptions, or does the change from token‑ to sequence‑level weighting alter the proofs? If so, how can we interpret the stability results observed in the paper from a theoretical standpoint?
